What Do We Actually Mean by AI Safety?

An assurance-oriented approach to evaluating deployed AI systems

AI safety claims are meaningful only when they specify the system, its intended use, the threat model, and the assumptions under which the claim is made. This paper approaches AI safety through assurance: the evidence that justifies confidence in a specified safety claim about a specified system. It distinguishes observation, evaluation, generalisation and impossibility claims; separates safety from security; explains why model evaluation is not equivalent to system evaluation; and examines sampling, search, verification, statistical limits, deployment shift, evaluator reliability and structural controls.

Introduction: what is the claim?

What do we actually mean by AI safety? Suppose tomorrow someone asks you to approve an AI system for your organisation and tells you, “Don’t worry, it’s been tested. It’s safe.” What exactly are they claiming, and what evidence would justify believing it?

This discussion approaches the question through assurance: how can we know whether an AI system is safe?

There are common answers that are useful but insufficient on their own: the system usually gives clean responses, refuses obviously harmful requests, or scores well on a benchmark. None of these answers, by itself, establishes what matters most: what evidence would justify the claim that this particular system is safe for this particular use?

The word particular matters. Assurance asks about a specific claim for a specific system and use, rather than whether “the AI” is safe in general.

There are many ways to approach AI safety, including alignment research, misuse, and wider effects on society. All matter. The focus here is narrower: what evidence justifies a particular safety claim about a particular deployed system?

A running example: the donor-administration agent

Imagine a charity deploys an AI agent to help with donor administration. It can read donor records, answer staff questions, query a database, and draft and send emails.

We give it one important instruction: do not disclose confidential donor information. This sounds like a safety property and might appear in a risk register as a control. But what has actually been established?

A system prompt is an instruction provided at inference time. It is text that the model conditions on when it runs. It is not a capability boundary, a security boundary, a permission boundary, or proof of impossibility.

Fine-tuning is different: it updates the model’s parameters and can change its behaviour, but it does not establish a mathematical invariant, a property guaranteed to hold in every case.

Suppose we test the model with the system prompt and it refuses to disclose a donor’s details. We know that, under that tested condition, it produced a refusal. That is evidence, but it is not a guarantee.

Now suppose we run 10,000 tests and the agent never leaks anything. Four different claims might be made:

  1. Observation: We did not see the failure in those 10,000 tests.
  1. Evaluation: The model passed the evaluation suite.
  2. Generalisation: The system will not disclose donor information in deployment.
  3. Impossibility: The system cannot disclose donor information.

Each claim requires a different kind of evidence. Much of the confusion in AI safety comes from moving from the first claim to the fourth without noticing.

Threat models: safe against what?

Before evaluating anything, we must ask: safe against what? This is the threat model. Possible threats include:

  • a benign user making an accidental request or phrasing something badly;
  • a malicious user deliberately trying to get around the rules;
  • prompt injection, where untrusted content ingested by the agent (such as an email or document) attempts to alter its behaviour;
  • plain model failure, where an unsafe action occurs without an adversary; and
  • hypothetical strategic subversion, where the system itself might game the evaluation or oversight.

A test suite built for the first scenario tells us very little about the last.

Safety and security also need to be kept apart. Safety concerns the system causing harm in its environment: system-to-environment. For example, the agent sends out confidential data. Security concerns an adversary compromising the system: adversary-to-system. For example, an attacker tricks the agent into sending out that data.

The two are linked: a security failure can become a safety failure, but a safety failure can also happen with no attacker involved. So they should be analysed separately, while keeping track of how one can lead to the other.

What exactly are we evaluating?

A user interacts with agent software. The agent calls the model, and the model returns a completion. The agent then acts through tools, such as a database. Between the agent and those tools sits a permission boundary that constrains which actions are allowed.

When someone says they evaluated the model, we should ask which component they actually evaluated. Evaluating the model’s outputs is not the same as evaluating the boundary around it.

Consider the same model deployed in two different systems:

  • System A: a read-only database, no internet, no email, and a human who approves every action;
  • System B: write access to the database, unrestricted email sending, memory between sessions, and autonomous action.

The model is the same, but the reachable states, consequences, and potential safety claims are very different. Evaluating the model does not automatically establish that the system is safe.

Models, agents, and trajectories

For an autoregressive model, the probability of a sequence factorises into a product of conditional probabilities. Each token (roughly, each word) is chosen with a probability that depends on all the tokens before it.

For a sequence x1, …, xT, this can be written as

P(x1, …, xT) = ∏t=1T P(xt | x1, …, xt−1)

Strictly speaking, the model defines a probability distribution over sequences, and stochasticity comes from sampling from it. With greedy decoding, the output is largely deterministic, though not entirely in practice. A single response is one realised trajectory through that process: effectively, one sample from the distribution. A failure might depend on the whole sequence, not just one isolated output.

For an agent, the picture is more complicated. Instead of a token sequence, we have a trajectory: a sequence of states and actions,

τ = (s1, a1, s2, a2, …, sn)

The state includes the conversation, the agent’s memory, tool outputs, its permissions, and the outside world. Actions include writing text, calling a tool, changing data, sending an email, or running code.

The trajectory is the whole run: what the agent saw, what it did, and what it saw next. This creates a feedback loop. The agent observes a state, selects an action, the action changes the environment, and the agent observes the new state and acts again.

Evaluation therefore becomes a sequential process of state, action, state, action, and so on. The action at step four is conditional on everything that happened at steps one to three.

Reachability and probability

Let U be the set of unsafe states. A trajectory reaches U if any state along it belongs to U. The first question is reachability: does there exist a trajectory that reaches U? In plain English, is there any path that ends somewhere bad?

The second question is probability: how likely is a run to hit a bad state? For a stochastic process, this can be expressed as

Pr(∃ t ∈ {1, …, n} : st ∈ U)

These are different questions. A state could be reachable and still have a very low probability of occurring. A probability is also always conditional on a specified stochastic process: which inputs, tools, and operating conditions are included?

There are at least eight different questions we might mean when we ask whether something is safe. These include observation (did we see a failure?), probability (how often does it occur under a stated process?), reachability (is an unsafe state possible at all?), and severity (how bad is it if it happens?). A single benchmark score does not answer all of these. Usually, it answers just one.

Sampling, searching, and verifying

Sampling, searching and verifying answer different questions:

  • Sampling asks what happened in the runs we happened to sample.
  • Search asks whether we can actively find a trajectory that reaches the failure.
  • Verification asks whether we can prove that no such trajectory exists under stated assumptions.

If we sample 10,000 trajectories and none reaches U, that tells us about the sample process. It does not establish that, for all trajectories, U is never reached, absent further assumptions or a proof. More sampling never turns into verification.

Red teaming goes looking for failures across the space of possible inputs and trajectories. Two dimensions matter: coverage, or how much of the relevant threat or state space is explored; and attack success, or how effectively the failure can be induced.

A test set can be very large and still cover a narrow region of the state space. An attack can be highly effective without providing broad coverage. More test cases do not necessarily mean more assurance if coverage remains narrow.

The statistical limits of testing

There is a standard statistical result called the rule of three. If n independent and identically distributed trials are run and zero failures are observed, the 95% upper confidence bound on the failure probability is approximately

pupper ≈ 3 / n

Our 10,000 clean tests therefore support a failure rate below approximately three in 10,000, or one in 3,333. To bound the failure rate below one in a million, we would need around three million failure-free trials.

These trials would also have to be independent and drawn from the deployment distribution: how the system is really used. So 10,000 clean test results cannot rule out a one-in-a-million failure.

Even if we could estimate probability, that would not be enough. Imagine System A fails once in every thousand runs, and the failure is a typo in a draft email. System B fails once in every million runs, but the failure is a catastrophic disclosure of donor data. System A fails a thousand times more often, but B’s failure is far worse.

We cannot decide how much assurance we need from frequency alone. A safety argument must connect probability, consequence, and exposure (how many opportunities the system has to fail), alongside the controls in place.

Evaluation as an experiment

Evaluation is an experiment. It has a population or process, a sampling mechanism, a test environment, an evaluator, a metric, and a set of assumptions.

When someone says a model scored 99%, six questions should follow:

  1. 99% of what?
  1. Under what conditions?
  1. Measured how?
  1. Against what ground truth?
  1. Marked by what evaluator?
  1. Relevant to what deployment?

If nobody can answer these questions, the 99% does not mean very much.

Most evaluations assume a fixed evaluation distribution: static prompts, independent test cases, and a controlled environment. This is useful, but it is an abstraction. Real deployment is different. Context changes, users adapt, the agent remembers things, and conversations run for a long time.

The relevant object may therefore be a trajectory distribution induced by an interactive system rather than a static collection of independent test cases. Fixed-distribution evaluation remains useful, provided we understand which abstractions it makes and whether they are adequate for the claim.

Evaluation and deployment

Pre-deployment evaluation tends to be curated, adversarially chosen, recognisable as a test, narrow, and short. Deployment is varied, interactive, long-running, adaptive, and partly unknown.

This is a generalisation problem: an inference from one data-generating process to another. So the question that matters is why passing the evaluation should tell us anything about the deployment we care about.

One response is to make evaluation look more like deployment. We can use realistic tool environments and mock databases whose state changes as real ones do. We can replay real, de-identified interaction prefixes, the openings of genuine conversations. We can also run long-horizon trajectories of 100 turns or more to test for information leakage over time.

This does not remove uncertainty. Rare failures are still difficult to sample, and future deployments may not look like past deployments. But it makes one point clear: the data-generating process is part of the assurance argument.

When the model knows it is being tested

What if the model knows it is being tested? In some cases, this may be obvious from the context, for example if the input says, “You are being evaluated for safety.” Research suggests that this information itself can change behaviour.

Research on sandbagging refers to strategic underperformance on evaluations. Work by van der Weij and colleagues shows that language models can be made to selectively underperform on some capability evaluations. This was demonstrated in specific experimental settings, where models were prompted or fine-tuned to do so; it does not show that deployed models routinely behave this way.

It does establish a methodological concern: the conditions under which we measure a system can affect the behaviour we observe.

There is another issue: the system doing the marking can also fail. Imagine the model says, “I complied with the safety policy.” An automated evaluator, often another language model acting as a judge, reads this and marks it as safe. In reality, the action had an unsafe side effect.

The chain now runs from model to output to evaluator to judgement. The evaluator is part of the assurance system and needs an assurance argument of its own.

Capability and measurement

Demonstrated capability is not the same as possessed capability. A model might have a capability but fail to exhibit it without specific prompting. This is why capability elicitation is its own problem.

Conversely, the semantic appearance of an output is not the same as its operational consequence. An output can look harmful without actually being harmful in effect. Observed behaviour is evidence about capability, but it is not a complete measure of it.

A 2025 example from Panfilov and colleagues brings these points together. They gave frontier models harmful requests. Some models responded with answers that looked harmful but had been quietly made useless. This fooled automated monitors, which scored them as successful attacks. The monitor was measuring the wrong thing and did not know.

The hopeful part of this work is that linear probes on the models’ internal activations could detect the fake answers, even where output-based checks failed.

If measurement can be systematically fooled, the measurement itself can become part of the safety problem. Looking inside the model can add evidence that outputs alone cannot provide.

The agent is situated

An agent does not act in a vacuum. Its behaviour depends on what its tools actually do and what it thinks they do; what its permissions allow; the instructions in its system prompt; what it remembers between sessions; who reviews its actions; and the data, users, and systems on which it acts.

If any of these change, behaviour can change. The unit of analysis is often the model within a system and an environment, rather than the model alone.

From behavioural safety to system control

What happens if we do not trust the model? Suppose it makes mistakes, encounters a prompt injection, or behaves differently outside the test conditions. Do we simply add another line to the prompt, or change the underlying architecture?

The first strategy is behavioural safety. We train or instruct the model to behave safely. This includes system prompts, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimisation methods such as RLHF, refusal training, and safety classifiers. These methods are useful, but the safety property depends on the model continuing to choose the right behaviour. The argument rests on the model.

The second strategy is structural safety, where we change what the system is able to do. The model requests a tool call; a policy check validates it against permissions; and a hard boundary can block any action that is not permitted.

Returning to the donor example, the model asks to call a function that sends an email with a donor record attached. The architecture refuses, regardless of what the model decided.

The safety claim now rests on what the system allows to happen, whatever the model decides, and that is much easier to check.

AI control

A deeper version of this idea is known as AI control. The paper by Greenblatt et al. (2024) sets out a blunt threat model: assume the model may be intentionally trying to subvert your safety measures.

Could you design a control protocol, comprising monitoring, checks, and review, that stays safe anyway? The design is meant to hold even if the model does not cooperate.

Verification and the specification problem

Testing is not verification. Testing says that we tried 10,000 inputs and saw no unauthorised database writes. Verification says that, given these permissions and system rules, an unauthorised write is unreachable.

The second is much stronger: it is a reachability result covering every trajectory the rules allow, including the ones nobody tried. It is also much more expensive to establish.

Verification proves a property of a model of the system, under stated assumptions. Whether the real world is safe depends on how well that model matches it.

Five questions should be asked about any proof:

  1. What exactly is the property?
  1. What abstractions of the system is it about?
  1. What are we assuming about the environment?
  1. Which interactions are represented?
  1. Does the formal property actually match the real safety requirement?

The assurance question is whether these provide good enough representations of the claim that we actually care about.

Suppose we formally prove that, for all trajectories, an unauthorised email is never sent. That is a genuine result. But the actual failure may be different: the agent may export the donor database through the SQL tool. The proof says nothing about that.

We would have proved the wrong property, correctly.

Assurance begins with the specification: deciding what we are trying to prevent in the first place.

Bringing the evidence together

When someone says that a model passed, they could mean four different things, in two categories.

Behavioural evidence concerns what the model did:

  • Evaluation: we did not see failures under the tested conditions.
  • Generalisation: we have reasons to think the same behaviour will hold in deployment.

Structural evidence concerns what the system allows:

  • Control: even if the model fails, the architecture limits the damage.
  • Guarantee: under explicit assumptions, the failure is ruled out.

These do not form a single ladder: no amount of behavioural evidence turns into a guarantee, and structural evidence does not depend on the model behaving at all.

There is no useful statement of the form “this model is safe” on its own. We must still ask: safe against what, for whom, in what environment, with what permissions, over what time period, under what threat model, with what consequences, and judged against what system?

A system can satisfy one safety claim and fail another. It can be right for one deployment and wrong for another without the model changing at all.

Conclusion: what exactly did it pass?

Assurance is evidence that justifies confidence in a specified safety claim about a specified system under specified assumptions.

The evidence can come from evaluation, adversarial testing, statistics, simulation, monitoring, red teaming, architectural controls, and more. No single one of these answers every safety question.

At the top of an assurance argument, we define the claim, the safety property, and the threat model. We then consider the deployed system and the trajectories it can produce. Finally, we bring together evidence from several sources.

Behavioural evidence includes sampling, search, and statistics. Operational evidence includes monitoring and incident data. Structural evidence includes control and verification. Each has its own assumptions.

Assurance is the argument that brings these sources together. It is only as strong as those assumptions and as the independence of the sources. If every layer can fail for the same reason, the layers do not add up.

Return, finally, to the donor agent. The claim was that the agent will not disclose confidential donor information. We now know what to ask: What counts as disclosure? Which model are we using? Which threats are we considering? Could the failure emerge only after several steps? What did we test? Did we actively search for failures? Why should we believe the tests represent real use? Could we detect a disclosure? Can the system technically prevent the export? Can we show that the permission boundary holds?

We now have an assurance programme problem. That is progress, because it is something we can work on.

Every time someone tells you that the model passed, ask what exactly it passed. What safety claims does that result support? What connects the test to the deployment? What happens outside the tested conditions? What if the evaluator is wrong? What if the failure is rare or reachable but simply never sampled?

So when a model passes, the question is what we actually know as a result.

An assurance-oriented approach to AI safety has to get much better at answering that question.
